sources.quote: The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 見(み)出(だ)す (midasu, “to find out, to select”).

pos: noun or participle which takes the aux. verb suru
headline: ノック covers “knock” and baseball fungo, and the source traces it to English “knock”.
終える traces a long sound path from Old Japanese wopu, through /wofuru/ and /oheru/, to /oeru/.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese verb wopu, from Proto-Japonic *wopu.

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

The root verb was ambitransitive, with both transitive and intransitive senses conjugated using the 下二段活用 (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern. Over time, the two senses differentiated as the intransitive evolved into modern 終わる (owaru, also derivable as the spontaneous or passive -aru ending from a putative but unrecorded 四段活用 (yodan katsuyō), the full quadrigrade conjugation pattern), while the transitive evolved into modern 終える (oeru, with the 下一段活用 (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) pattern, also known as "type 2", and the expected historical development for shimo nidan verbs).
Probably not related to superficially similar 追う (ou, ancient opu, “to follow”, quadrigrade conjugation in older Japanese), considering the distinct lack of initial /w/ in ancient spellings.

株, “stock; stump (of tree)”, is from Old Japanese, with cognates in Kunigami, Amami Ōshima and Okinawan.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kampu. Cognate with Kunigami 株 (khabū), Northern Amami Ōshima 株 (gabu), Okinawan 株 (kabu).

headline: スケート is the English word “skate” in katakana.
琴, “Japanese harp”, is possibly a compound of 木 (ko, “tree, wood”) and 音 (oto, “sound”), with a medial o dropped.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, attested in the three major literature works of the Nara period: the Kojiki (712 CE), the Nihon Shoki (720 CE), and the Man'yōshū (c. 759 CE).
Possibly derived from a compound of elements 木 (ko, “tree, wood”, combining form) + 音 (oto, “sound”), with the additional medial o dropped by haplology.

headline: 泊める is a doublet of 止める (tomeru).
ウイスキー is borrowed from the English spelling “whisky”.
若々しい doubles 若 (waka) and adds the suffix しい (-shii).

sources.quote: Reduplication of 若(わか) (waka), the stem of 若(わか)い (wakai, “young”), suffixed with しい (-shii).

headline: コンサート is borrowed from English “concert”.
“You” began as a place word: あなた originally meant that direction, that side, that place far away.

sources.quote: Compound of あ (a, distal pronoun marker, indicating something far away from both speaker and listener; also found in あれ (are, “that”, far away), あそこ (asoko, “there”, far away), etc.) + な (na, possessive, ancient compounding alternative for (and possibly derived from) particle の (no)) + た (ta, “direction, side, place”, only found in ancient terms; possibly contracted from 方 (kata)).

Originally meant that direction, that side, that place (far away), in contrast to そなた (sonata, “that direction, that side, that place (closer to the listener)”), こなた (konata, “this direction, this side, this place (close to both listener and speaker)”), and どなた (donata, “which or what direction, side, or place”). Appears with this sense at least as early as the Kokin Wakashū of the late 900s, and the Kagerō Nikki of 974 CE.
The indirect and polite sense of that person is also evident in texts from the late 900s, including the Ochikubo Monogatari.
The sense of you as a polite and indirect form of reference appears in texts from around the 1750s.

headline: ミルク is borrowed from English “milk” and first cited in the 1870s.
ハンカチ is borrowed from English “handkerchief”.
地, “earth”, is a kan'on reading, and the source suspects a dialectal source for its devoiced initial.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 地 (dijᴴ). The kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing. The devoicing of the initial consonant might indicate a dialectal source. Compare modern Hakka thi, Min Nan tī.

headline: 通じる is a shift from the verb 通ずる (tsūzuru).

sources.quote: Shift from verb 通(つう)ずる (tsūzuru), by natural progression from サ行変格活用 (sa-gyō henkaku katsuyō, “s-irregular conjugation”) verbs ending in -uru to 上一段活用 (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.

headline: ギャング is the English word “gang” in katakana.

meaning: ogre, demon, 'it' (e.g.,in a game of tag)
headline: 鬼, “ogre, demon”, is thought to derive from 隠 (on, “to hide; hidden from sight”).

sources.quote: Thought to be derived from 隠(おん) (on, “to hide; hidden from sight”).
